en.title: Political Science: the whole course
en.short: The BSc and MSc course: theory, comparative politics, international relations, policy, Africa and methods.

sections.heading: What the field is
sections.text:
Political science is the systematic study of power, government and collective decisions. It asks who rules, how they came to rule, why people obey, what rulers do, and what difference institutions make. Harold Lasswell summed up one view in the title of his 1936 book, Politics: Who Gets What, When, How. David Easton offered another when he defined politics as the authoritative allocation of values for a society.

The field has two broad sides. Empirical work tries to explain what happens, using evidence. Normative work asks what should happen, using argument. A strong student keeps these questions apart, and also sees how they connect.

sections.heading: How a degree is usually organised
sections.text:
A first degree takes four years at most Nigerian and Ghanaian universities and often three in the UK. Master’s programmes usually last one or two years. Nigerian programmes follow National Universities Commission benchmarks, and each university adds its own courses. Polytechnics more often teach this material through public administration diplomas.

Early courses introduce the discipline and its main thinkers. Later courses go deeper into each subfield, often with a country focus. Most final-year students write a research project. Master’s students take advanced theory and methods, choose a specialism and write a dissertation.

sections.heading: The main areas in teaching order
sections.text:
These topics follow a common order:
Foundations: the discipline, and the concepts of power, the state and legitimacy.
Political thought: classical, medieval, early modern and modern thinkers, then African political thought and contemporary theory.
Political behaviour: opinion, voting and participation, then parties and electoral systems.
Comparative politics: methods, regimes and institutions.
International relations: basic concepts, theories, foreign policy and global governance.
Public administration and public policy: classical theory, reform, and how policies are made and implemented.
Political economy: states, markets, dependency, development and natural resources.
Africa and Nigeria: the postcolonial state, constitutional development and federal politics.
Methods: research design and data analysis.
Master’s level: advanced theory, comparative democratisation and security studies.

sections.heading: How to study it
sections.text:
Read the original thinkers as well as textbooks. A short passage of Hobbes or Fanon, read with care, teaches more than a list of claims about them. For each theory, write down its central claim, its assumptions, its best evidence and its strongest critic.

Then apply the theory to a case. Pick two or three countries that you know well and use them throughout your course. Compare them with cases from another region, so that you can see which patterns are general and which are local. Learn basic statistics early, because much published research now uses it.

Facts about current politics change quickly. Treat any dated fact in these summaries as correct only at the date given, and check recent events against official sources and your lecturer’s reading list.

sections.heading: Common mistakes
sections.text:
These errors cost marks at every level:
Describing institutions without making an argument.
Giving your own political opinion in place of evidence.
Presenting one scholar’s view as settled when the question is contested.
Treating correlation as proof of cause.
Generalising from a single country, or treating Africa as one case.
Confusing the normative question with the empirical one.
Using a concept such as democracy or the state without defining it.
Attributing a view to a thinker without knowing the text. Machiavelli, for example, did not write the phrase that the end justifies the means in those words.

A good answer defines its terms, sets out the competing views fairly, weighs the evidence and then reaches a reasoned conclusion. These summaries are neutral guides. They do not tell you which party, leader or theory to support.

keyPoints: Political science studies power, government and collective decisions.
Empirical questions ask what happens. Normative questions ask what should happen.
The main subfields are theory, comparative politics, international relations, public administration and policy.
Good answers define terms, set out rival views and weigh evidence.
Check any fact about current politics against its date and an official source.

en.title: Political science as a discipline
en.short: What counts as politics, how the discipline developed, and its main approaches and subfields.

sections.heading: What counts as politics
sections.text: Scholars disagree about the boundaries of the subject. A narrow definition limits politics to government and the state. A wider one finds politics wherever power is used and contested, including in families, firms and religious bodies. Feminist writers made this wider view famous with the slogan that the personal is political. The choice of definition decides what you study, so state yours clearly.

sections.heading: How the discipline developed
sections.text:
Early study was philosophical, legal and historical. It described constitutions and asked about the best form of rule. In the 1950s and 1960s, the behavioural movement, strongest in the United States, moved attention from formal rules to what people actually do. It valued measurement and testable claims. Easton’s systems theory treated politics as a process in which demands and support enter a political system and policies come out.

Around 1969, Easton himself described a post-behavioural reaction. Critics said that the field had become technical and had neglected urgent problems. Since the 1980s, new institutionalism has returned to institutions. James March and Johan Olsen argued in 1984 that institutions shape what actors want and how they behave.

sections.heading: Main approaches today
sections.text:
Rational choice assumes that actors pursue goals in a consistent way, and it models the results. Historical institutionalism traces how early choices limit later ones, an idea called path dependence. Constructivist and interpretive work studies how ideas and meanings shape action. Marxist approaches stress class and the economy. Feminist approaches ask how gender shapes power.

Each approach sees some things clearly and misses others. Example: to explain why a coalition collapses, a rational choice scholar looks at each party’s incentives, while a historical institutionalist looks at the rules and past bargains behind it.

keyPoints: Politics can be defined narrowly, as the state, or widely, as all contested power.
Behaviouralism shifted attention from formal rules to observable conduct.
Easton defined politics as the authoritative allocation of values.
New institutionalism argues that institutions shape behaviour and preferences.
Path dependence means that early choices limit later ones.

en.title: Theories of power, the state and legitimacy
en.short: The faces of power, rival theories of the state, and how scholars explain legitimacy.

sections.heading: Three views of power
sections.text:
Robert Dahl (1957) offered a direct test: A has power over B to the extent that A can get B to do something that B would not otherwise do. To find power, watch who wins open decisions.

Peter Bachrach and Morton Baratz (1962) replied that power also works by keeping issues off the agenda. A council that never debates land rights may be showing power, not agreement.

Steven Lukes (1974) added a third dimension. Power can shape what people want, so that they accept arrangements that harm them and never raise a complaint. Critics ask how an observer can know a person’s real interests. Michel Foucault took a different line. He treated power as spread through everyday practices and forms of knowledge, not held by one group.

sections.heading: Rival theories of the state
sections.text:
Max Weber defined the modern state by its means: it claims a monopoly of the legitimate use of physical force within a territory. Other theories ask whom the state serves.
Pluralists see the state as an arena where many groups compete and no group always wins.
Elite theorists, such as Gaetano Mosca, Vilfredo Pareto and C. Wright Mills, argue that a small minority always rules.
Marxists see the state as tied to the interests of the dominant class, though some allow it relative autonomy.
Feminists examine how the state has built gender inequality into law and policy.

sections.heading: Legitimacy
sections.text: Weber’s approach is descriptive: a regime is legitimate if people believe that it has the right to rule. David Beetham (1991) argued that belief is not enough. Power must also follow established rules that can be justified by shared beliefs, and it must receive expressed consent. Scholars also separate input legitimacy, which comes from fair procedures, from output legitimacy, which comes from good results.

keyPoints: Dahl studied decisions. Bachrach and Baratz studied agendas. Lukes studied how preferences are shaped.
Weber defined the state by its claim to a monopoly of legitimate force.
Pluralist, elite and Marxist theories disagree about whom the state serves.
Input legitimacy comes from procedures, and output legitimacy from results.
Foucault saw power as spread through practices and knowledge.

en.title: Classical and medieval political thought
en.short: Plato, Aristotle, Cicero, Augustine, Aquinas, al-Farabi, Ibn Khaldun and early thinkers in Asia.

sections.heading: Ancient Greece and Rome
sections.text:
Plato, in the Republic, argued that justice means each part of society doing its proper work. He wanted philosophers to rule, because only they know the good. He distrusted democracy, which had condemned his teacher Socrates. Critics, notably Karl Popper in 1945, saw an authoritarian danger in this vision.

Aristotle studied many constitutions. He classified them by who rules and in whose interest. Rule by one, few or many for the common good gives monarchy, aristocracy and polity. Rule for the rulers’ own good gives tyranny, oligarchy and democracy. He favoured a polity with a large middle group. He also defended slavery and the rule of men over women, and modern readers must weigh this.

The Roman writer Cicero argued that a natural law, known through reason, stands above the laws of any state.

sections.heading: Medieval Christian and Islamic thought
sections.text:
Augustine of Hippo, from North Africa, contrasted the earthly city with the city of God. He expected no perfect justice from any government. Thomas Aquinas joined Aristotle to Christian belief. He set out four kinds of law: eternal, natural, human and divine.

Al-Farabi (about 870 to 950) drew on Plato to describe a virtuous city led by a wise ruler. Ibn Khaldun, born in Tunis in 1332, wrote the Muqaddimah. He explained the rise and fall of dynasties through asabiyyah, or group solidarity. Solidarity helps a group to win power, and then comfort and luxury weaken it over generations. Many scholars regard him as an early social scientist.

sections.heading: Beyond the Mediterranean
sections.text: Courses increasingly widen the canon. Confucius, in China, stressed rule by moral example. The Arthashastra, a text linked to Kautilya in ancient India, offers practical advice on statecraft. Its date and authorship are debated.

keyPoints: Plato wanted philosopher-rulers and distrusted democracy.
Aristotle classified constitutions by who rules and in whose interest.
Natural law holds that a higher law, known by reason, judges human law.
Aquinas set out eternal, natural, human and divine law.
Ibn Khaldun explained dynastic cycles through asabiyyah, or group solidarity.

en.title: Early modern thought: Machiavelli to Rousseau
en.short: Machiavelli, Hobbes, Locke and Rousseau in depth, with modern critiques of the social contract.

sections.heading: Machiavelli
sections.text: Niccolò Machiavelli wrote The Prince around 1513. He separated political success from conventional virtue. A ruler needs virtù, meaning skill and boldness, to master fortuna, meaning chance. Readers disagree sharply. Some see a teacher of ruthlessness. Others, such as Quentin Skinner, stress his Discourses and read him as a republican concerned with liberty and civic life.

sections.heading: Three versions of the contract
sections.text:
Hobbes, Locke and Rousseau all begin with an imagined state without government, but they reach different results because they assume different things.

Thomas Hobbes, in Leviathan (1651), assumes rough equality and scarce security. Fear leads to a war of all against all. People therefore give almost all their rights to a sovereign, keeping only the right to preserve their own lives.

John Locke, in the Second Treatise (1689), assumes a natural law that already gives rights. People form government for greater security, so it holds power on trust. A government that breaks that trust may be resisted. His account of property, gained by mixing labour with land, was later used to justify taking land in the Americas, and scholars debate how far that use follows from his own argument.

Jean-Jacques Rousseau, in The Social Contract (1762), thinks that society itself has corrupted people. Freedom means obeying laws that you help to make. The general will aims at the common good and differs from the will of all, which is only a sum of private interests. Isaiah Berlin and others warned that his phrase about forcing people to be free could serve tyranny.

sections.heading: Modern critiques
sections.text: Carole Pateman, in The Sexual Contract (1988), argued that the classic contract assumed the subordination of women. Charles Mills, in The Racial Contract (1997), argued that it worked in practice as an agreement among white people that excluded others. Defenders reply that the contract idea can correct these faults, and they point to later egalitarian versions.

keyPoints: Machiavelli separated political success from conventional virtue, and his meaning is disputed.
Hobbes’s fear of disorder leads to a nearly absolute sovereign.
Locke’s government holds power on trust and may be resisted.
Rousseau’s general will differs from the will of all.
Pateman and Mills argue that the contract excluded women and non-white people.

en.title: Modern thought: Burke, Mill, Tocqueville and Marx
en.short: Conservatism, utilitarianism, liberalism, the tyranny of the majority, Marxism and its successors.

sections.heading: Tradition and utility
sections.text:
Edmund Burke, in Reflections on the Revolution in France (1790), warned against rebuilding society from abstract theory. He treated inherited institutions as stored wisdom and favoured gradual reform. His writing became a founding text of conservatism.

Jeremy Bentham took the opposite line. He judged laws by their results, using the principle of the greatest happiness of the greatest number. This is utilitarianism. Mary Wollstonecraft (1792) argued that women’s apparent weakness came from poor education, and she claimed equal rights for women on grounds of reason.

sections.heading: Liberalism and democracy
sections.text:
John Stuart Mill, in On Liberty (1859), set out the harm principle: society may restrict a person’s liberty only to prevent harm to others. He defended free debate because even false views help us to test what we believe. Critics ask what counts as harm. Others note that he accepted colonial rule over peoples he judged not yet ready for self-government.

Alexis de Tocqueville studied the United States and published Democracy in America in 1835 and 1840. He admired local self-government and voluntary associations. He also feared the tyranny of the majority, in which public opinion crushes dissent even without laws.

sections.heading: Marx and after
sections.text:
Karl Marx, working with Friedrich Engels, argued that history moves through conflicts between classes, defined by their relation to the means of production. This view is called historical materialism. Under capitalism, workers sell their labour, and owners keep the surplus value that it creates. Marx expected workers to overthrow this system.

Later Marxists adjusted the theory. V.I. Lenin stressed a disciplined party and explained imperialism as a stage of capitalism. Antonio Gramsci asked why workers in the West had not revolted. He answered with hegemony: dominant classes rule partly by winning consent through culture, schools and media. Critics of Marxism point to the failure of predicted revolutions and to the record of states that claimed to follow it. Defenders separate his analysis from those states.

keyPoints: Burke defended inherited institutions and gradual reform.
Utilitarianism judges actions by their results for overall happiness.
Mill’s harm principle limits interference with individual liberty.
Tocqueville warned about the tyranny of the majority.
Gramsci’s hegemony means rule through consent as well as force.

en.title: Comparative politics: method and regime types
en.short: Why and how political scientists compare countries, and how they classify regimes.

sections.heading: Why compare
sections.text: Comparative politics studies politics within countries by setting cases side by side. Comparison helps us to test explanations, because we cannot usually run experiments on whole states. It also shows that what looks natural in one country is a choice that others made differently.

sections.heading: The logic of comparison
sections.text:
John Stuart Mill’s logic underlies two common designs.
In a most similar design, cases share many features but differ in the outcome. The researcher looks for the factor that also differs.
In a most different design, cases differ in many ways but share an outcome. The researcher looks for the factor they have in common.

Example: Daniel Posner (2004) studied Chewa and Tumbuka people on both sides of the Zambia and Malawi border. Their cultures are alike, yet the groups are political opponents in Malawi and allies in Zambia. He explained this by size. Each group is large relative to Malawi’s politics, and small relative to Zambia’s. Size relative to the political arena shapes whether cultural difference matters.

Comparison has known traps. With few cases and many variables, several explanations may fit. Giovanni Sartori (1970) warned against conceptual stretching, which means widening a term until it fits everything and explains nothing.

sections.heading: Classifying regimes
sections.text:
A regime is the set of rules that decides how power is won and used. It usually outlasts any one government. Juan Linz distinguished authoritarian regimes, which allow limited pluralism and do not require mass ideological commitment, from totalitarian regimes, which seek total ideological control.

Barbara Geddes (1999) grouped authoritarian regimes into personalist, military and single-party types. She argued that they break down differently. Military regimes often return to barracks by negotiation, while personalist regimes may end more violently. Many classifications now treat regimes as a scale, not as fixed boxes, and the master’s topic on democratisation takes this further.

keyPoints: Comparison helps to test explanations when experiments on states are impossible.
A most similar design seeks the factor that differs among similar cases.
A most different design seeks the factor shared among different cases.
Conceptual stretching widens a term until it loses its meaning.
A regime is the set of rules for winning and using power.

en.title: International relations: basic concepts
en.short: Anarchy, sovereignty, actors, levels of analysis, forms of power and the basis of international law.

sections.heading: The international system
sections.text:
International relations (IR) studies conduct across state borders. Its starting point is anarchy. In IR, this does not mean chaos. It means that no world government stands above states to make and enforce rules.

Textbooks often date the system of sovereign states to the Peace of Westphalia of 1648. Some historians, such as Andreas Osiander, call this a myth, because the treaties did not create sovereignty as it is now understood. For much of the world, the sovereign state arrived only through colonial rule and decolonisation.

sections.heading: Actors and levels of analysis
sections.text:
States are the main actors, but they are not alone. Others include international organisations, multinational companies, non-governmental organisations and armed groups.

Kenneth Waltz (1959) asked why wars happen and looked for causes at three levels: human nature, the internal character of states, and the international system. J. David Singer (1961) made levels of analysis a basic tool of the field. Example: a border war can be explained by a leader’s personality, by domestic politics, or by a regional balance of power. A strong essay says which level it uses.

sections.heading: Power and interest
sections.text:
Hard power means getting results through force or payment. Joseph Nye’s term soft power means getting results through attraction, such as culture and values. Critics say that soft power is hard to measure.

The balance of power can mean several things: a distribution of power, a policy of opposing a rising rival, or a stable state of affairs. National interest is what a state’s leaders say it needs. Scholars debate whether it is objective or built by domestic politics.

sections.heading: International law
sections.text: Article 38 of the Statute of the International Court of Justice lists the sources applied by that court: treaties, custom and general principles of law, with judicial decisions and scholarly writing as subsidiary means. Article 2(4) of the UN Charter prohibits the threat or use of force between states. The main exceptions are self-defence and action authorised by the Security Council.

keyPoints: Anarchy means the absence of a world government, not chaos.
Westphalia (1648) is the usual starting date, but historians dispute it.
Waltz located causes of war in individuals, states and the system.
Soft power works through attraction, not force or payment.
Treaties and custom are the main sources of international law.

en.title: Public administration: classical to human relations
en.short: Wilson’s dichotomy, Weber’s bureaucracy, scientific management, Hawthorne and Simon’s critique.

sections.heading: Founding ideas
sections.text:
Public administration studies how governments put decisions into effect. Woodrow Wilson’s essay of 1887 argued that administration should be a field of study in its own right, separate from politics. This idea, the politics-administration dichotomy, shaped early thinking. Dwight Waldo and others later argued that administrators also make political choices, because applying a rule involves judgement.

Max Weber described bureaucracy as an ideal type, meaning a simplified model. It has a clear hierarchy, written rules, specialised offices, appointment by qualification and careers separated from personal ownership. Weber saw it as technically efficient and also feared its power to confine human life. Robert Merton (1940) noted a dysfunction: officials may come to treat following the rule as the goal itself.

sections.heading: Classical management
sections.text: Frederick Taylor (1911) proposed scientific management: study each task, find the best method, and pay according to output. Henri Fayol (1916) described the work of managers and set out 14 principles, such as unity of command. Luther Gulick (1937) summed up executive duties in the word POSDCORB: planning, organising, staffing, directing, coordinating, reporting and budgeting.

sections.heading: Reaction and critique
sections.text:
The Hawthorne studies at a Western Electric factory in the United States, begun in the 1920s and associated with Elton Mayo, suggested that social ties and attention affect work. This inspired the human relations school. Later scholars have questioned how the original data were read. Douglas McGregor (1960) contrasted Theory X, which assumes that workers avoid effort, with Theory Y, which assumes that they can seek responsibility.

Herbert Simon (1947) attacked classical principles as proverbs, because they often contradict each other. He argued that administrators work with limited information and time. They satisfice, which means choosing an option that is good enough.

keyPoints: Wilson’s dichotomy separates politics from administration, and later writers challenged it.
Weber’s bureaucracy is an ideal type with hierarchy, rules and merit.
POSDCORB sums up the classical view of executive work.
The Hawthorne studies inspired attention to social factors at work.
Simon argued that administrators satisfice under bounded rationality.

en.title: African political thought
en.short: Pan-Africanism, Négritude, African socialism, Fanon, Cabral and debates on consensus democracy.

sections.heading: Early and anti-colonial thought
sections.text:
African political ideas long predate colonial rule. In the Sokoto Caliphate, founded in the early nineteenth century, Uthman dan Fodio wrote on just Islamic government. Edward Blyden and J.E. Casely Hayford, writing in West Africa, defended African institutions and identity against European claims. Nnamdi Azikiwe and Obafemi Awolowo produced nationalist writing in Nigeria, and Awolowo’s Path to Nigerian Freedom (1947) made an early case for federalism.

Kwame Nkrumah argued that political independence would mean little without continental unity. In Neo-Colonialism (1965), he said that outside powers can still direct a formally independent state through economic means. Léopold Senghor and Aimé Césaire developed Négritude, which asserted the value of black culture. Wole Soyinka and others criticised it as a mere reaction to European categories.

sections.heading: African socialism and liberation
sections.text:
Julius Nyerere’s ujamaa, meaning familyhood, sought a socialism rooted in African communal life. Supporters praise its ethics and its contribution to national unity. Critics cite the economic results and the coercion used in villagisation in Tanzania during the 1970s.

Frantz Fanon, in The Wretched of the Earth (1961), analysed the violence of colonial rule and warned that a national middle class might simply replace the colonisers. His view of violence is still debated. Amílcar Cabral stressed that liberation needs theory fitted to local conditions, and culture as a source of resistance. Steve Biko’s Black Consciousness in South Africa stressed psychological liberation.

sections.heading: Philosophical debates
sections.text: Kwasi Wiredu proposed a non-party democracy based on consensus, drawing on Akan practice. Critics, including Emmanuel Eze, doubt that consensus was so common and fear that it can silence dissent. Paulin Hountondji criticised ethnophilosophy, which treats a whole people as sharing one philosophy. Writers on ubuntu see persons as formed through relations with others. Oyèrónkẹ́ Oyěwùmí, in The Invention of Women (1997), argued that gender was not an organising category in Yoruba society before colonial rule. Others dispute this reading.

keyPoints: Nkrumah linked independence to unity and warned about neo-colonialism.
Négritude asserted the value of black culture, and it was criticised as reactive.
Nyerere’s ujamaa sought an African form of socialism.
Fanon warned that a national middle class could replace colonial rulers.
Wiredu’s consensus democracy has both defenders and critics.

en.title: Contemporary theory: justice, liberty and ideology
en.short: Rawls, Nozick, communitarians, capabilities, feminist theory, two concepts of liberty and populism.

sections.heading: Debates about justice
sections.text:
John Rawls, in A Theory of Justice (1971), asks what principles people would choose behind a veil of ignorance, not knowing their own class, talents or beliefs. He argues for equal basic liberties, fair equality of opportunity and the difference principle. That principle allows inequalities only if they benefit the worst off.

Robert Nozick (1974) replied that justice concerns how holdings were acquired, not their pattern. If people gained their goods fairly, taxing them for redistribution is a wrong. Communitarians such as Michael Sandel, Michael Walzer and Alasdair MacIntyre object that Rawls’s chooser has no community or history. Amartya Sen and Martha Nussbaum ask a different question: what are people actually able to do and be? This is the capabilities approach. Susan Moller Okin (1989) asked why theories of justice left out the family.

sections.heading: Liberty and recognition
sections.text:
Isaiah Berlin (1958) separated negative liberty, the absence of interference, from positive liberty, being one’s own master. He feared that positive liberty could justify coercion in the name of a person’s true self. Others think that the division is too sharp.

Will Kymlicka (1995) argued that liberal justice can support group rights for minority cultures. Nancy Fraser distinguished injustices of distribution from injustices of recognition.

sections.heading: Ideology today
sections.text:
Michael Freeden (1996) treats ideologies as patterns that arrange concepts such as liberty and equality in different ways. This helps to explain why liberals differ among themselves. Neoliberalism favours markets and a limited economic role for the state. Supporters credit it with growth and efficiency, and critics link it with inequality. Ecologism challenges the priority of economic growth.

Cas Mudde (2004) calls populism a thin ideology that sets a pure people against a corrupt elite, and it can attach to left or right. Ernesto Laclau treats it as a logic of political speech and sees democratic potential in it. Scholars still disagree on whether populism threatens democracy or renews it.

keyPoints: Rawls’s difference principle allows inequality only if it benefits the worst off.
Nozick judges justice by how holdings were acquired.
The capabilities approach asks what people can actually do and be.
Berlin separated negative from positive liberty.
Mudde defines populism as a thin ideology of people against elite.

en.title: Political behaviour, culture and participation
en.short: How people form opinions, why they vote or protest, and what research in Africa adds.

sections.heading: Culture and opinion
sections.text: Political socialisation is how people acquire political views, through family, school, peers, religion and media. Gabriel Almond and Sidney Verba, in The Civic Culture (1963), surveyed five countries and described parochial, subject and participant orientations. They argued that democracy is most stable in a mixed culture. Critics said that the model favoured the United States and Britain as the standard. Ronald Inglehart argued that rising security shifts values towards self-expression. Afrobarometer, whose surveys began in 1999, gives comparable data on African opinion.

sections.heading: Why people vote as they do
sections.text:
Three classic models compete. The sociological model, from Paul Lazarsfeld’s Columbia studies in the 1940s, stresses social groups. The Michigan model, from The American Voter (1960), stresses long-term party identification. The rational choice model of Anthony Downs (1957) sees voters as comparing expected benefits.

Downs’s model raises the paradox of voting. One vote rarely decides an election, yet millions vote. Answers include a sense of civic duty and social pressure.

In African settings, research has looked at ethnicity and clientelism, meaning the exchange of goods or favours for political support. Leonard Wantchekon (2003) ran a field experiment during an election in Benin, and clientelist appeals generally outperformed policy-based appeals. Eifert, Miguel and Posner (2010) found that people across ten countries identified more with ethnic groups close to competitive elections. Other scholars show that voters also judge performance, so ethnicity is not the whole story.

sections.heading: Participation beyond voting
sections.text:
Mancur Olson (1965) showed why large groups struggle to act: each person gains from a shared benefit without paying for it. Social movement theories explain how people overcome this. Relative deprivation theory stresses grievance. Resource mobilisation theory stresses organisation and money.

Turnout varies widely. In Nigeria’s 2023 presidential election, about 25 million voters were accredited out of about 93 million registered, or about 27 percent. Scholars debate the reasons, including insecurity, trust and the accuracy of registers.

keyPoints: Almond and Verba described parochial, subject and participant cultures.
The main voting models are sociological, party identification and rational choice.
The paradox of voting asks why people vote when one vote rarely decides.
Clientelism is the exchange of goods or favours for political support.
Olson’s problem is that individuals can enjoy shared benefits without helping.

en.title: Political parties and party systems
en.short: Types of party, the iron law of oligarchy, measures of party systems, and party politics in Africa.

sections.heading: Types and organisation
sections.text:
Maurice Duverger (1951) contrasted cadre parties, run by small groups of notables, with mass parties built on large memberships. Otto Kirchheimer (1966) described catch-all parties, which reduce ideology to seek votes from every group. Richard Katz and Peter Mair (1995) described cartel parties, which rely on state funding and limit competition among themselves.

Robert Michels (1911) proposed the iron law of oligarchy: any large organisation, however democratic in its aims, comes to be run by a few. Internal primaries are one answer, and scholars debate how well they work.

sections.heading: Where party systems come from
sections.text: Seymour Lipset and Stein Rokkan (1967) argued that Western European party systems grew from social divisions, called cleavages: centre against region, church against state, land against industry, and owners against workers. Later scholars ask whether these patterns travel. In Africa, Rachel Riedl (2014) linked party system stability to how authoritarian rulers handled local elites before multi-party politics returned. Nicolas van de Walle (2003) described a common pattern of a large party around the president with small, fluid opponents.

sections.heading: Counting and classifying
sections.text:
Sartori (1976) argued that counting parties is not enough. We must also ask which parties matter and how far apart they stand. His types include predominant systems and polarised pluralism.

The effective number of parties, by Laakso and Taagepera (1979), weights parties by size: N = 1 ÷ Σs², where s is each party’s share.
Example: shares of 0.5, 0.3 and 0.2.
Σs² = 0.25 + 0.09 + 0.04 = 0.38
N = 1 ÷ 0.38 ≈ 2.6

sections.heading: Recent cases
sections.text: Dominant parties can lose. The Botswana Democratic Party, in office since independence, lost the October 2024 election. South Africa’s African National Congress lost its majority in May 2024, winning 159 of 400 seats, and then formed a Government of National Unity with other parties. In Ghana, power passed between two main parties again in December 2024. Eighteen parties ran presidential candidates in Nigeria in 2023.

keyPoints: Party types include cadre, mass, catch-all and cartel.
Michels’s iron law says large organisations come to be run by a few.
Lipset and Rokkan traced party systems to social cleavages.
Effective number of parties: N = 1 ÷ Σs².
Sartori classified systems by the number of relevant parties and their distance.

en.title: Electoral systems and electoral integrity
en.short: How seats are allocated, Duverger’s law, electoral engineering, quotas and electoral manipulation.

sections.heading: Seat allocation
sections.text:
Proportional systems need a formula for turning votes into seats. The D’Hondt method divides each party’s votes by 1, 2, 3 and so on, then gives seats to the highest results in turn.
Example: 5 seats. Votes are A 42,000, B 31,000, C 18,000 and D 9,000.
A: 42,000, 21,000, 14,000
B: 31,000, 15,500
C: 18,000, 9,000
D: 9,000
The five highest are 42,000, 31,000, 21,000, 18,000 and 15,500.
Result: A 2, B 2, C 1, D 0.
D’Hondt tends to favour larger parties slightly. Sainte-Laguë, with divisors 1, 3, 5, is more even-handed between large and small parties.

sections.heading: Effects of electoral systems
sections.text:
Duverger’s law says that single-member plurality systems tend towards two parties, for two reasons. The system under-rewards small parties, and voters avoid wasting votes. Proportional systems tend to allow more parties. The tendency is not universal. India and Canada have more than two significant parties under plurality rules, often because support is regionally concentrated.

Electoral engineering means designing rules to get certain results. Nigeria and Kenya add geographic spread requirements for presidents, to encourage a broad national base. Nigeria’s has existed since the 1979 Constitution. Donald Horowitz favours rules that reward appeals across groups, while Arend Lijphart favours proportional representation for divided societies. Gender quotas are another tool. Rwanda’s 2003 Constitution reserves at least 30 percent of seats in decision-making bodies for women.

sections.heading: Integrity and manipulation
sections.text:
Andreas Schedler (2002) described a menu of manipulation, including excluding opponents, limiting their campaigns, buying votes and fraud on the day. Pippa Norris studies electoral integrity across the whole cycle, not only polling day.

Nigeria’s Electoral Act 2026, signed on 18 February 2026, replaced the 2022 Act. INEC’s revised timetable of February 2026 then set presidential and National Assembly elections for 16 January 2027 and state elections for 6 February 2027. Courts ruled on party primaries and deadlines during 2026. As far as could be confirmed in November 2026, none changed these dates. Check INEC’s website.

keyPoints: D’Hondt divides votes by 1, 2, 3 and allocates seats to the highest results.
Duverger’s law links plurality rule with two-party systems, with exceptions.
Electoral engineering designs rules to shape outcomes.
Nigeria and Kenya require geographic spread for presidents.
Schedler’s menu shows that manipulation happens long before polling day.

en.title: Comparing institutions and federal design
en.short: Lijphart’s democracies, the presidentialism debate, consociationalism, federal theory and courts.

sections.heading: Majoritarian and consensus democracy
sections.text:
Arend Lijphart (1999) compared democracies along a set of institutional features. Majoritarian systems, on the Westminster model, concentrate power in a one-party cabinet. Consensus systems, as in Switzerland and Belgium, share it through coalitions, proportional representation and federalism. He claimed that consensus systems match majoritarian ones on governing performance and do better on representation. Critics question his measures and his case selection.

His earlier theory of consociationalism offered a recipe for divided societies: grand coalition, mutual veto, proportionality and autonomy for each group. Donald Horowitz replies that this can harden group identities, and he prefers rules that reward moderation across groups. Scholars weigh both in cases such as Lebanon, Bosnia and Burundi.

sections.heading: The presidentialism debate
sections.text: Juan Linz (1990) argued that presidential systems are riskier for democracy. Both president and legislature claim a popular mandate, and fixed terms leave no easy exit from conflict. Winner takes all, which raises the stakes. Matthew Shugart and John Carey (1992) replied that the details of presidential power matter more than the label. José Cheibub (2007) argued that presidential democracies die more often because they tend to follow military dictatorships, not because of the system itself. Semi-presidentialism, a term popularised by Maurice Duverger, has its own debate, on whether a divided executive causes conflict.

sections.heading: Theories of federalism
sections.text: K.C. Wheare (1946) gave a legal test: central and regional governments are each independent within their own sphere. William Riker (1964) saw federalism as a bargain, made by politicians to meet a military or diplomatic threat. Alfred Stepan (1999) distinguished coming-together federations, such as the United States, from holding-together federations, such as India, where the centre shares power to keep a diverse state intact. Scholars debate whether federalism reduces ethnic conflict or gives it a stronger base.

sections.heading: Courts
sections.text: Ran Hirschl (2004) describes juristocracy, a shift of major decisions to judges. Supporters say that courts protect rights and limit majorities. Others see a loss of democratic control.

keyPoints: Lijphart contrasts majoritarian and consensus democracy.
Consociationalism shares power among groups, and Horowitz offers an alternative.
Linz warned about presidentialism, and Cheibub disputes the causal claim.
Wheare’s test is legal, and Riker’s explanation is a political bargain.
Stepan contrasts coming-together and holding-together federations.

en.title: Theories of international relations
en.short: Realism, liberalism, the English School, constructivism, critical, feminist and postcolonial theories.

sections.heading: Realism
sections.text: Realists take states and power as central. Hans Morgenthau (1948) rooted the struggle for power in human nature. Kenneth Waltz (1979) moved the cause to the structure of the system. Under anarchy, states must look after their own security. Defensive realists think that states seek enough security. John Mearsheimer (2001), an offensive realist, argues that great powers seek as much power as they can. Critics say that realism struggles to explain peaceful change, such as the end of the Cold War.

sections.heading: Liberalism and the English School
sections.text:
Liberals think that cooperation can grow, even under anarchy. Robert Keohane (1984) argued that institutions make cooperation easier by sharing information and reducing the costs of agreement. Keohane and Joseph Nye described complex interdependence. Michael Doyle (1983), drawing on Immanuel Kant, developed democratic peace theory: democracies rarely fight each other. Critics question the definitions used and the direction of cause.

The English School, with Hedley Bull’s The Anarchical Society (1977), holds that states form a society with shared rules, even without a government.

sections.heading: Constructivist and critical views
sections.text:
Alexander Wendt (1992) argued that anarchy is what states make of it. Threat depends on identities and shared meanings, not on material power alone. Finnemore and Sikkink traced how norms spread.

Critical theories ask whose interests a theory serves. Robert Cox (1981) wrote that theory is always for someone and for some purpose. Immanuel Wallerstein’s world-systems theory divides the world economy into core, semi-periphery and periphery. Feminist writers, such as Cynthia Enloe and J. Ann Tickner, show how gender shapes war, diplomacy and labour.

sections.heading: Global South perspectives
sections.text: Amitav Acharya and Barry Buzan asked why non-Western IR theory has so little recognition. Kevin Dunn and Timothy Shaw (2001) argued that African experience challenges theories built around strong states. Many African states rest on legal recognition more than on control of their territory. Many argue that IR’s basic assumptions come from European history. Good essays use theories as tools, and ask what each one explains in a chosen case.

keyPoints: Neorealism explains state conduct through the structure of anarchy.
Liberal institutionalism argues that institutions make cooperation easier.
Democratic peace theory says that democracies rarely fight each other.
Wendt argued that anarchy is what states make of it.
Critical, feminist and postcolonial theories ask whose experience IR theory reflects.

en.title: Foreign policy and global governance
en.short: How foreign policy is explained, Nigeria’s foreign policy record, and debates on global institutions.

sections.heading: Explaining foreign policy
sections.text: Foreign policy analysis opens up the state and asks how decisions are made. Graham Allison, in Essence of Decision (1971), examined the Cuban missile crisis through three models. In the rational actor model, a state chooses the option that best serves its goals. In the organisational process model, decisions follow the routines of agencies. In the governmental politics model, they result from bargaining among officials.

sections.heading: A case: Nigeria
sections.text:
Nigerian foreign policy is usually taught around a principle that Africa is its centrepiece, a phrase tied to the policy review of the mid-1970s. Examples often cited include support for liberation movements in southern Africa and leadership of ECOMOG, the ECOWAS force sent to Liberia in 1990 and later to Sierra Leone. Ibrahim Gambari later described national interests as concentric circles, with Nigeria’s own security and its neighbours at the centre, then West Africa, then the continent.

Assessments differ. Some writers credit these policies with regional stability and prestige. Others question the costs at home and the limited return to Nigeria. In a territorial dispute, the International Court of Justice ruled in 2002 that the Bakassi peninsula belonged to Cameroon. Nigeria transferred the area in 2008 under the Greentree Agreement. Many scholars cite this as peaceful dispute settlement, and affected residents raised concerns.

sections.heading: Global governance
sections.text:
Global governance means rules and coordination across borders without a world government.

Debates focus on representation. In the Ezulwini Consensus of 2005, the African Union called for at least two permanent African seats on the UN Security Council, with all the powers of existing members, and further non-permanent seats. Supporters say that the present structure reflects 1945. Others warn that enlargement could make decisions harder. Regional bodies are also under strain. Burkina Faso, Mali and Niger, which formed the Alliance of Sahel States in September 2023, left ECOWAS with effect from 29 January 2025. Talks on cooperation resumed in October 2026. Analysts disagree on what this means for regional integration.

keyPoints: Allison’s three models are rational actor, organisational process and governmental politics.
Africa as centrepiece is a classic framing of Nigerian foreign policy.
The ICJ ruled on Bakassi in 2002, and Nigeria transferred it in 2008.
The Ezulwini Consensus sets out the African Union’s position on Security Council reform.
Burkina Faso, Mali and Niger left ECOWAS on 29 January 2025.

en.title: Public policy: making and implementing it
en.short: The policy cycle, models of decision-making, agenda-setting, implementation and evaluation.

sections.heading: What policy is
sections.text: Thomas Dye defined public policy as whatever governments choose to do or not to do. So inaction can be policy too. Theodore Lowi (1964) sorted policies into distributive, regulatory and redistributive types, and argued that each creates its own kind of politics. Teachers often use a policy cycle: agenda-setting, formulation, adoption, implementation and evaluation. Real policy rarely follows such neat stages.

sections.heading: How decisions are made
sections.text:
The rational-comprehensive model expects decision-makers to list all options and choose the best. Herbert Simon replied that limits on knowledge and time produce bounded rationality. Charles Lindblom (1959) called real policymaking muddling through, with small steps from the existing position. Critics say that incrementalism favours the status quo. Amitai Etzioni’s mixed scanning combines a broad review with detailed study of a few options.

John Kingdon (1984) explained agenda-setting with three streams: problems, policies and politics. When they join, a policy window opens. Baumgartner and Jones (1993) described punctuated equilibrium, meaning long periods of stability broken by sudden change. Paul Sabatier’s advocacy coalition framework studies groups that share beliefs over long periods.

Example: South Africa introduced a levy on sugary drinks in 2018. A Kingdon-style analysis could trace concern about obesity, the available tax design, and the political conditions that allowed adoption.

sections.heading: Implementation and evaluation
sections.text:
Pressman and Wildavsky (1973) showed how a federal programme in Oakland, California, weakened as it passed through many decision points. Top-down scholars ask how to make officials follow the plan. Bottom-up scholars look at those who deliver it. Michael Lipsky (1980) argued that street-level bureaucrats, such as teachers, police and nurses, effectively make policy through their daily choices.

Evaluation asks whether a policy caused its result. This requires a counterfactual, an estimate of what would have happened without the policy. Example: comparing enrolment before and after a fee change, as in Ghana’s Free Senior High School policy from 2017, does not settle the question alone, since other changes happen at the same time.

keyPoints: Dye’s definition includes what governments choose not to do.
Lindblom’s incrementalism describes small steps from the existing position.
Kingdon’s policy window opens when problems, policies and politics join.
Lipsky’s street-level bureaucrats shape policy through daily choices.
Evaluation needs a counterfactual to show what a policy caused.

en.title: Administrative reform and development administration
en.short: New Public Management, governance, Riggs and Ekeh on African states, and civil service reform.

sections.heading: From administration to management
sections.text:
From the 1980s, New Public Management (NPM) sought to bring private sector methods into government. Its tools include performance targets, contracting out and semi-independent agencies. Christopher Hood (1991) described and questioned this trend. Supporters claim gains in efficiency and service. Critics argue that citizens are not simply customers and that targets can distort work. Results vary by sector and country.

Other approaches followed. Governance writers stress networks of state, market and civil society actors. Mark Moore’s public value asks managers to create results that the public cares about.

sections.heading: Administration in developing states
sections.text: Fred Riggs (1964) built a model of prismatic society, in which formal rules exist alongside older social ties, so formal rules do not predict conduct well. Peter Ekeh (1975) argued that colonialism created two publics in Africa. The primordial public, based on kin and community, carries moral duties. The civic public, linked with the state, does not. So an official may divert public funds to his home community and still be seen as moral there. Critics warn that such models can over-generalise and neglect political incentives.

sections.heading: Reform in practice
sections.text:
Nigeria offers a long series of reforms. The Udoji Commission (1974) recommended a results-based service and higher pay. The 1988 Civil Service Reforms gave ministers a larger role and changed the post of permanent secretary, and later reviews reversed parts of them. Section 14(3) of the 1999 Constitution sets out the federal character principle, under which appointments should reflect the country’s diversity. Supporters see inclusion and national unity. Critics worry about effects on merit. Others say that the two can be combined.

Constitutions elsewhere state values directly. Section 195 of South Africa’s Constitution and Article 232 of Kenya’s set out principles for public administration and public service. Merilee Grindle argues that agendas for good governance are often too long. She proposes good enough governance, which sets priorities in light of each country’s capacity.

keyPoints: NPM brought targets, contracting out and agencies into government.
Riggs’s prismatic society mixes formal rules with older social ties.
Ekeh’s two publics are the primordial and the civic.
Nigeria’s reforms include Udoji (1974) and the 1988 Civil Service Reforms.
Section 14(3) of Nigeria’s 1999 Constitution sets out federal character.

en.title: Political economy and development
en.short: States and markets, dependency, developmental states, adjustment and the resource curse.

sections.heading: States and markets
sections.text: Political economy studies how power and wealth shape each other. Robert Gilpin (1987) described three traditions. Liberals, following Adam Smith and David Ricardo, stress the gains from trade. Economic nationalists, or mercantilists, stress state power and protected industry. Marxists stress class and exploitation. Karl Polanyi (1944) argued that markets are always embedded in society, so that attempts to free them provoke protective reactions. Friedrich Hayek, also in 1944, warned that central planning threatens liberty.

sections.heading: Dependency and its critics
sections.text: Modernisation theorists saw all societies moving along a shared path to development. Dependency writers rejected this. Raúl Prebisch and Hans Singer argued that the terms of trade for primary exports tend to decline. André Gunder Frank wrote of the development of underdevelopment. Walter Rodney, in How Europe Underdeveloped Africa (1972), held that European trade and colonial rule actively damaged African economies. Critics point to East Asian growth and to domestic causes. Fernando Cardoso and Enzo Faletto argued that some development can occur within dependence.

sections.heading: Paths of state action
sections.text:
Chalmers Johnson (1982) described Japan as a developmental state, in which a skilled bureaucracy guides industry. Peter Evans (1995) called the winning combination embedded autonomy. Scholars disagree on whether this model can be repeated in Africa.

Robert Bates (1981) argued that African governments taxed farmers to reward urban and political allies. The World Bank’s Berg Report of 1981 and the structural adjustment programmes that followed, in Ghana from 1983 and Nigeria from 1986, reduced state roles. Defenders cite restored growth, as in parts of Ghana’s record. Critics, including Thandika Mkandawire, cite social costs and weak industrial results.

sections.heading: Natural resources
sections.text: The resource curse is the claim that resource wealth can harm development and politics. A rentier state lives on outside income, so it needs little tax and may answer less to citizens. Michael Ross links oil to weaker democracy. Others question this finding, and Botswana’s diamond record is a common counterexample. Institutions may be the deciding factor, a view associated with Acemoglu, Johnson and Robinson.

keyPoints: Gilpin’s three traditions are liberal, nationalist and Marxist.
Rodney argued that Europe actively underdeveloped Africa.
A developmental state guides industry through a skilled bureaucracy.
A rentier state lives on outside income, such as oil revenue.
Botswana is a common counterexample to the resource curse.

en.title: African politics: the postcolonial state
en.short: Juridical statehood, neopatrimonialism, the colonial legacy, one-party rule, coups and term limits.

sections.heading: Theories of the state in Africa
sections.text: Robert Jackson and Carl Rosberg (1982) argued that many weak African states survive because of juridical statehood, meaning international recognition, even where empirical statehood, meaning real control, is limited. Jeffrey Herbst (2000) traced this to the difficulty of projecting power over large, thinly settled land. Mahmood Mamdani, in Citizen and Subject (1996), argued that colonial rule built a divided state: civil law for urban citizens and customary authority for rural subjects. Claude Ake stressed that colonial power was absolute and that elites inherited it.

sections.heading: The neopatrimonial debate
sections.text: Neopatrimonialism describes a system with formal legal offices where power also flows through personal networks. Bratton and van de Walle used it in studying Africa’s transitions. Jean-François Bayart’s politics of the belly describes how elites and their followers share access to state resources. Thandika Mkandawire (2015) challenged this approach. He argued that it cannot explain variation in economic performance and that it can rest on stereotypes.

sections.heading: Changing regimes
sections.text: After independence, many states moved to one-party or military rule. Leaders defended single parties as tools of national unity, while critics saw limits on rights. A wave of change followed around 1990, opened in part by Benin’s national conference in that year. Multi-party elections spread quickly. Posner and Young (2007) noted that leaders increasingly left power by formal routes. Debates over presidential term limits have followed in many states.

sections.heading: Military takeovers since 2020
sections.text: Takeovers occurred in Mali, Chad, Guinea, Sudan, Burkina Faso, Niger and Gabon between 2020 and 2023, and in Madagascar and Guinea-Bissau in late 2025. Attempts failed in Benin (2025) and Niger (2026). The African Union has rules against unconstitutional change, in its Constitutive Act and in the African Charter on Democracy, Elections and Governance (2007), and it has suspended states on this basis. Explanations include insecurity, disputed elections and term extensions, rivalry within armed forces, and foreign influence. Scholars also debate why some takeovers gain public support. This list was checked in November 2026, so look for later events.

keyPoints: Juridical statehood rests on recognition, and empirical statehood on real control.
Mamdani argued that colonial rule divided citizens from subjects.
Neopatrimonialism mixes formal offices with personal networks.
Mkandawire challenged neopatrimonial explanations of economic performance.
The African Union can suspend states after unconstitutional changes of government.

en.title: Nigerian constitutional development
en.short: From the 1914 amalgamation to the 1999 Constitution and later alterations, compared with other states.

sections.heading: The colonial constitutions
sections.text:
In 1914, Frederick Lugard joined the Northern and Southern Protectorates. Later constitutions added representation step by step.
Clifford, 1922: introduced elected seats, for Lagos and Calabar.
Richards, 1946: created regional houses.
Macpherson, 1951: strengthened regional government after wider consultation.
Lyttelton, 1954: established a federal structure.

The Willink Commission (1957 to 1958) studied the fears of minorities and advised against creating new states before independence.

sections.heading: From independence to 1999
sections.text:
The 1960 Independence Constitution was followed by the 1963 Republican Constitution, which ended appeals to the Privy Council and replaced the Queen with a president. After the first 1966 coup, the Unification Decree tried to end federalism, and it was reversed after the second. Twelve states replaced the regions in 1967. The number reached 36 in 1996. A presidential system was adopted in the 1979 Constitution. The 1989 Constitution was prepared for a Third Republic that did not fully begin, and the presidential election of June 1993 was annulled.

The 1999 Constitution was brought into force by a military decree. Its opening words, which present it as made by the people, have led some scholars and activists to question its legitimacy and to call for a new constitution. Others argue that it has been accepted through use and amendment.

sections.heading: Alteration
sections.text: Under section 9, most alterations need two-thirds of each federal chamber and of the state assemblies. Alterations in 2018 lowered age limits for office, and those of 2023 moved railways and other matters to the Concurrent List. A state police bill went to state assemblies in September 2026. By November, at least 30 had reportedly approved it, above the 24 required, but it was not yet law. Check for later steps.

sections.heading: Comparison
sections.text: South Africa negotiated an interim constitution in 1993, and its Constitutional Court certified the 1996 text. Ghana approved its 1992 Constitution and Kenya its 2010 Constitution by referendum. H.W.O. Okoth-Ogendo (1991) described constitutions without constitutionalism, meaning that a text exists but does not truly limit rulers.

keyPoints: Clifford introduced elected seats, Richards regions, and Lyttelton a federal structure.
The 1979 Constitution adopted a presidential system.
The 1999 Constitution came into force through a military decree.
Section 9 sets out how the 1999 Constitution is altered.
Constitutionalism means that a constitution truly limits rulers.

en.title: Nigerian politics: federalism, ethnicity and the republics
en.short: The republics, military rule, prebendalism, revenue allocation, zoning and local government debates.

sections.heading: Republics and military rule
sections.text:
The First Republic, usually dated from independence to January 1966 (Nigeria became a republic only in 1963), saw three regional power bases and crises over the census and elections of 1962 to 1965. Two coups in 1966 were followed by the Civil War of 1967 to 1970. The Second Republic ran from 1979 to 1983. The Fourth Republic began in 1999.

Scholars explain the instability differently. Some stress competition among political elites and a federation in which one region outweighed the others. Larry Diamond (1988) analysed the link between class formation and ethnic conflict. Richard Joseph (1987) introduced prebendalism, in which public offices are treated as sources of benefit for holders and their groups. Critics say that this concept can suggest a fixed national culture and overlook change.

sections.heading: Federalism and money
sections.text:
Rotimi Suberu (2001) studied how Nigeria’s federal arrangements both contain and generate conflict. Disputes concern state creation, census results, and revenue. Section 162(2) of the 1999 Constitution requires that at least 13 percent of revenue from natural resources go to the states that produce them. This is the derivation principle. Producing states and their advocates seek more control, while others point to national unity and to the needs of poorer states.

The debate on restructuring asks whether powers should be moved from the centre to lower levels. Nigeria’s Supreme Court ruled on 11 July 2024 that councils should receive federal allocations directly. Reports through 2026 describe implementation as incomplete.

sections.heading: Power-sharing and security
sections.text:
Informal zoning rotates offices among regions in many parties. Some see it as a stabilising bargain, and others say that it limits voters’ choice.

Security has become a central theme. Examples are the Niger Delta conflict, which led to an amnesty programme in 2009, the Boko Haram insurgency in the north-east since about 2009, and rural violence in several regions. Scholars relate these to many causes, including inequality, weak state presence, climate pressure and ideology. They weigh those causes differently.

keyPoints: Joseph’s prebendalism treats public office as a source of group benefit.
Section 162(2) requires a derivation share of at least 13 percent.
Restructuring means moving power from the centre, and its meaning is contested.
Zoning is an informal rotation of offices within parties.
The Supreme Court’s 2024 ruling on councils was reported as incompletely implemented through 2026.

en.title: Research methods: designing a study
en.short: Research questions, hypotheses, variables, case studies, sampling, surveys, interviews and ethics.

sections.heading: From question to hypothesis
sections.text:
A good research question is specific, can be answered with evidence, and matters beyond the case. Compare “Why is politics corrupt?” with “Why did council spending rules vary among three Nigerian states after 2015?” A hypothesis is a testable claim about how two things relate.

A variable is a feature that changes across cases. The dependent variable is what you want to explain. The independent variable is what you think explains it. A confounder affects both and can create a false link. Operationalisation means deciding how to measure a concept. Democracy might be measured through free elections, civil liberties, or an index. Measures should be reliable, which means consistent, and valid, which means measuring what they claim to.

sections.heading: Research designs
sections.text:
Experiments randomly assign a treatment, so that groups differ only by chance. Survey and field experiments are common in political science, though not all questions allow them. Observational studies use data from events as they occurred.

Case studies examine one or a few cases in depth. Process tracing, described by Alexander George and Andrew Bennett (2005), follows the causal steps within a case. King, Keohane and Verba (1994) argued that qualitative and quantitative research share one logic of inference. Brady and Collier (2004) replied that qualitative research has strengths of its own. Many projects use mixed methods.

sections.heading: Collecting data
sections.text:
A sample is the group studied, chosen from a population. In random sampling, every member has a known chance of selection. Other methods include stratified sampling, which fixes shares for each group, and purposive sampling, which picks informants for what they know.

Common sources include surveys, elite interviews, focus groups, documents, archives and election data. Each has risks. People may give socially acceptable answers, and official records may be incomplete.

Ethics matters at all stages. Obtain informed consent, protect respondents’ identity and avoid harm, especially in conflict zones or under repressive rule. Most universities require ethical approval before fieldwork.

keyPoints: The dependent variable is what you explain, and the independent variable explains it.
A confounder affects both variables and can create a false link.
Valid measures capture the concept, and reliable measures are consistent.
Process tracing follows causal steps within a case.
Informed consent and protecting respondents are basic ethical duties.

en.title: Research methods: analysing political data
en.short: Margins of error, chi-square, regression, causal inference and qualitative analysis, with worked examples.

sections.heading: Margins of error
sections.text:
A poll reports an estimate with uncertainty. For a random sample and a share near 50 percent, the 95 percent margin of error is about 1.96 × √(p(1 − p) ÷ n).
Example: n = 1,000 and p = 0.5.
1.96 × √(0.25 ÷ 1,000) = 1.96 × 0.0158 ≈ 0.031
This is about 3 percentage points. If a candidate polls 48 percent and a rival 46 percent, the survey does not clearly separate them. Margins do not cover other errors.

sections.heading: Testing a relationship
sections.text:
A chi-square test asks whether two categories are related in a table.
Example: 200 respondents. Of 100 urban people, 60 voted and 40 did not. Of 100 rural people, 40 voted and 60 did not. If the two variables were unrelated, each cell would expect 50.
χ² = Σ (observed − expected)² ÷ expected
Each cell gives 10² ÷ 50 = 2, so χ² = 4 × 2 = 8.
With one degree of freedom, the 5 percent critical value is 3.84. Since 8 exceeds 3.84, the result is statistically significant. This shows that chance alone is unlikely to explain the difference. It does not show that the difference is large or important, or what caused it.

Regression estimates how an outcome changes with one variable while holding others constant. It controls only for what you measure.

sections.heading: Causal inference
sections.text: Correlation is not causation. The link may run the other way, or a confounder may explain both. Newer designs seek stronger evidence. Difference in differences compares change over time in a group affected by a policy with change in a group that was not. Natural experiments use chance events or arbitrary borders.

sections.heading: Qualitative analysis
sections.text: Content analysis counts or codes themes in texts, such as party manifestos. Discourse analysis asks how language builds meaning and power. Thematic coding organises interview material. Good practice includes clear coding rules, a search for evidence against your own view, and triangulation, which means checking one source against others.

keyPoints: A random sample of 1,000 has a margin of error of about 3 percentage points.
A significant result is unlikely to come from chance alone, but it may be small.
Regression controls only for the variables you measure.
Difference in differences compares change in treated and untreated groups.
Triangulation means checking one source against others.

en.title: Advanced political theory
en.short: Contextualism, Arendt, Habermas, Schmitt and Mouffe, Foucault, republicanism and postcolonial theory.

sections.heading: Method in theory
sections.text: Quentin Skinner (1969) argued that a text must be read as an act within its own historical debate, not as a timeless answer. Critics of this contextualism say that it can shrink the texts’ value for present questions. Charles Mills (2005) attacked ideal theory, which models a perfectly just society, as hiding actual oppression. Defenders reply that we need an ideal to judge reality.

sections.heading: Democracy: reason and conflict
sections.text:
Hannah Arendt, in The Human Condition (1958), treats politics as action among equals in a public space. She distinguishes it from labour and from work.

Jürgen Habermas grounds democratic legitimacy in discourse. Between Facts and Norms (published in German in 1992) holds that laws are legitimate if those affected could agree to them in rational debate.

Carl Schmitt defined the political through the distinction between friend and enemy, and he attacked liberal parliamentary politics. His support for the Nazi regime complicates his reception. Chantal Mouffe borrows from him but rejects his conclusion. In her agonism, opponents are adversaries, not enemies, and conflict is a healthy part of democracy. She argues that deliberative theory underrates passion and exclusion. Deliberative theorists respond that without some shared standards, conflict has no fair limit.

sections.heading: Power, freedom and the postcolonial
sections.text:
Michel Foucault, in Discipline and Punish (1975), traced how modern institutions shape conduct through surveillance and norms. Critics question whether this view leaves room for resistance.

Philip Pettit (1997) revives a republican idea of freedom as non-domination. A person with a kind master is still unfree, because the master could interfere at will.

Postcolonial theory questions the universal claims of Western thought. Edward Said’s Orientalism (1978) studied how Western knowledge constructed the East. Gayatri Spivak asked whether the voices of the most marginalised can be heard in such discourses. Achille Mbembe’s On the Postcolony (2001) studies power and everyday life in African postcolonial states. Critics such as Vivek Chibber argue that this tradition neglects material interests and shared human struggles.

keyPoints: Skinner reads texts as acts within their historical debates.
Habermas grounds legitimacy in rational discourse.
Mouffe’s agonism treats opponents as adversaries, not enemies.
Pettit defines freedom as non-domination.
Postcolonial theory questions the universal claims of Western thought.

en.title: Comparative democratisation
en.short: Measuring democracy, explanations of transition, hybrid regimes, backsliding and African experience.

sections.heading: Defining and measuring
sections.text: Joseph Schumpeter (1942) offered a minimal definition: democracy is a competition for votes among leaders. Robert Dahl (1971) described polyarchy, with two dimensions: contestation and inclusion. Fuller definitions add civil liberties and the rule of law. Measures reflect these choices. Polity scores regimes on a scale from −10 to +10. Freedom House rates political rights and civil liberties. V-Dem produces separate indices for different conceptions of democracy.

sections.heading: Why transitions happen
sections.text:
Seymour Lipset (1959) linked democracy to economic development. Adam Przeworski and Fernando Limongi (1997) argued that wealth mainly helps democracies to survive, and does not cause transitions. Boix and Stokes (2003) replied that development also promotes transition.

Barrington Moore (1966) stressed class coalitions and wrote that without a bourgeoisie there is no democracy. Rueschemeyer, Stephens and Stephens (1992) gave the working class the key role. O’Donnell and Schmitter (1986) focused on elite bargains within regimes. Samuel Huntington (1991) described a third wave of transitions, beginning in Portugal in 1974. In Africa, Bratton and van de Walle (1997) stressed protest from below and the character of each prior regime.

sections.heading: Beyond transition
sections.text:
Linz and Stepan (1996) described consolidation as the point at which democracy is the only game in town. Thomas Carothers (2002) attacked the transition paradigm, which assumed that countries move in one direction. Many stay in a grey zone.

Steven Levitsky and Lucan Way described competitive authoritarianism, in which real elections are held but the field is tilted towards incumbents. Staffan Lindberg (2006) argued that repeated elections in Africa themselves improve civil liberties over time.

sections.heading: Backsliding debate
sections.text: Nancy Bermeo (2016) described how democratic erosion has moved from sudden coups towards gradual changes by elected leaders. Levitsky and Ziblatt (2018) stress the erosion of informal norms. Little and Meng (2024) question how widespread the decline is, because objective indicators show less of it than expert ratings do. Others defend the expert measures, so this remains an open debate about evidence.

keyPoints: Dahl’s polyarchy rests on contestation and inclusion.
Przeworski and Limongi say wealth mainly sustains democracy, and Boix and Stokes disagree.
Huntington’s third wave began in Portugal in 1974.
Competitive authoritarianism has real elections on a tilted field.
The extent of backsliding depends partly on how it is measured.

en.title: Security studies
en.short: Widening security, securitisation, the security dilemma, civil war, peacekeeping and African security.

sections.heading: What is security
sections.text:
Traditional security studies focused on states and military threats. John Herz (1950) and Robert Jervis (1978) explained the security dilemma: one state’s defensive build-up can frighten another, so that both end up less secure.

Barry Buzan widened the agenda to political, economic, social and environmental sectors. The UN Development Programme’s 1994 report proposed human security, which makes the person the object of protection. Roland Paris (2001) argued that the term is too vague to guide research. The Copenhagen School, with Ole Wæver, developed securitisation: an issue becomes a security issue when a speaker presents it as an existential threat and an audience accepts this, which may justify emergency measures. Critics say that this focus on speech ignores other practices.

sections.heading: Why civil wars happen
sections.text: Paul Collier and Anke Hoeffler (2004) contrasted greed and grievance. Their work suggested that opportunities to fund rebellion predict civil war better than grievances do. James Fearon and David Laitin (2003) stressed conditions that favour insurgency, such as weak states and rough terrain, and they found ethnic diversity a weak predictor. Frances Stewart and others replied that inequality between groups matters.

sections.heading: Response and African cases
sections.text:
UN peacekeeping is traditionally based on consent, impartiality and limited force. Page Fortna (2008) found that peacekeeping substantially reduces the risk of renewed war. The Responsibility to Protect, endorsed at the UN in 2005, holds that states must protect their populations, and that others may act through the Security Council if a state manifestly fails. Supporters see an advance. Critics, recalling Libya in 2011, fear selective use.

The African Union’s Constitutive Act, article 4(h), allows intervention in cases of war crimes, genocide and crimes against humanity. Scholars debate regional forces against insurgents in the Lake Chad Basin, the Sahel and Somalia, and the mix of military action, governance and development that lasting security needs. The definition of terrorism remains contested in law and scholarship.

keyPoints: The security dilemma means that defensive steps can frighten others.
Human security makes the person the object of protection.
Securitisation presents an issue as an existential threat.
Collier and Hoeffler contrasted greed and grievance in civil war.
Article 4(h) of the AU Constitutive Act allows intervention in grave circumstances.
